first.label: supported
first.says: Casa Vicens, in Gràcia, is considered Gaudí's first major project; it was built between 1883 and 1885.
quote: is a modernist building situated in the Gràcia neighbourhood of Barcelona. It is the work of architect Antoni Gaudí and is considered to be his first major project. It was built between 1883 and 1885

town.label: supported
town.says: When it was built, Gràcia was still an independent town with its own council; it joined Barcelona in 1897.
quote: When the building was constructed, Gràcia was still an independent urban nucleus of Barcelona; it had its own council and was classified as a town
The town was added to Barcelona in 1897

unesco.label: verified
unesco.says: Casa Vicens is one of the Works of Antoni Gaudí on the UNESCO World Heritage list, added in 2005.
quote: the Casa Vicens, the Nativity Façade
in 2005 the Nativity façade, the crypt and the apse of Sagrada Família, Casa Vicens and Casa Batlló

sensation.label: supported
sensation.says: Here Gaudí first tried ideas that became regular features of Modernisme; the house caused a great sensation at the time.
quote: In this work, and for the first time, Gaudí outlined some of his constructive resources that would become regular features throughout the emergence of Modernisme. The work was widely discussed when it was built and caused a great sensation among the general public at the time.

client.label: supported
client.says: In 1878 Manuel Vicens i Montaner, a stock and currency broker about whom little is known, commissioned a summer house in Gràcia.
quote: In 1878 Gaudí received a commission from Manuel Vicens i Montaner to build a summer residence for the family in the town of Gràcia. Manuel Vicens (1836–1895) was a stock and currency broker, although there is little information about him.

flowers.label: supported
flowers.says: The tiles show yellow flowers Gaudí found growing on the site; a palmetto palm there inspired the gate. Gaudí's own words describe both.
quote: “When I went to take the measurements of the site, it was totally covered with some yellow flowers, which I used as an ornamental theme for the ceramic. I also found an exuberant palmetto palm, whose leaves fill the grid of the gate of the house”.

gate.label: supported
gate.says: At the street entrance is the gate with palm leaves and carnations: Gaudí detailed the design, Llorenç Matamala made a plaster mold, and Joan Oñós cast it in iron.
quote: At the entrance to the street is the gate decorated with palm leaves and carnation flowers designed by Matamala and made by Oñós.

The design of the gate was detailed by Gaudí in the plan of the facade that is kept in the Historical Archive of Catalonia, signed by Gaudí and Vicens on January 15, 1883. Using this design, sculptor Llorenç Matamala made a plaster mould, which was later cast in iron by forger Joan Oñós.

walls.label: supported
walls.says: The walls alternate masonry with tiles, some with plant motifs and some in a green and white check.
quote: Masonry ashlars alternate with the tiles, some with plant motifs and others in a green and white check design.

orient.label: supported
orient.says: It belongs to Gaudí's orientalist period, inspired by the Near and Far East (India, Persia, Japan) and by Hispanic Islamic art such as Mudéjar and Nasrid.
quote: an era in which the architect made a series of works with a distinctly oriental flavour, inspired by the art of the Near and Far East (India, Persia, Japan), as well as Hispanic Islamic art, such as Mudéjar and Nasrid.

serra.label: supported
serra.says: Seen from Carrer de les Carolines, the right half, which sticks out slightly, is Joan Baptista Serra's extension of 1925-1927; Gaudí alternated the tiles, Serra laid them uniformly.
quote: Serra built the right half of the building; seen from Carrer de les Carolines, and visible because it protrudes slightly onto the street, unlike the part built by Gaudí. The division is also noticeable by the different design of the tiles; Gaudí alternated them to give greater dynamism, while Serra arranged them in a uniform fashion. The extension took place between 1925 and 1927.

declined.label: supported
declined.says: Gaudí declined the extension because he was devoting himself fully to the Sagrada Família, and recommended his protégé Serra.
quote: He approached Gaudí to lead the project to extend the house, but he declined, as he was devoting himself fully to the Sagrada Família at the time. Instead, he recommended one of his protégés, Joan Baptista Serra

parasol.label: supported
parasol.says: According to Serra's testimony, Gaudí sat under a parasol supervising, sometimes knocking down work he thought poor.
quote: according to the testimony of Joan Baptista Serra to George R. Collins in 1959, the architect sat under a parasol and supervised the build, occasionally knocking down what he considered to be poor workmanship.

nation.label: supported
nation.says: In an unpublished 1881 article Gaudí wrote: 'The house is the small family nation.'
quote: an unpublished article he wrote in 1881
‘The house is the small family nation.

gardenfront.label: supported
gardenfront.says: The main facade in Gaudí's design looked onto the garden, on the southwest side.
quote: the main facade looked out onto the garden, on the southwest side

porch.label: supported
porch.says: The porch opened to the garden through oriental-style wooden latticework reminiscent of Japanese shitomi shutters; Gaudí could learn about this system at an 1881 exhibition in Barcelona.
quote: connected to the garden by oriental-inspired wooden latticework

it is inspired by the orient and reminiscent of a style of Japanese shutters called shitomi. Gaudí was able to learn about this system at an exhibition of Japanese architecture held in Barcelona in 1881.

fountain.label: supported
fountain.says: The porch fountain let water fall in a thin sheet that showed rainbow colors; it was later removed, and the restoration recovered it.
quote: The fountain allowed the water to flow as a thin sheet which reflected the colours of the rainbow when light passed through it.
The water fountain was also recovered, as in Gaudí’s original project.
The water fountain, one of the most evocative elements of Gaudí’s project, was also removed.

songs.label: supported
songs.says: The porch frieze carries Catalan folk-song lines: 'From the hearth, the fire, long live the fire of love' on the southwest wall, 'Sun, little sun, come and see me' on the southeast side, 'Oh, the shade of summer' on the northwest side.
quote: On the frieze of the covered porch there are a selection of phrases from Catalan folk songs: “Sol, solet, vinam a veure” (“Sun, little sun, come and see me”) on the southeast side; “Oh, l’ombra de l’istiu” (“Oh, the shade of summer”) on the northwest side
“De la llart lo foch, visca lo foch de l'amor” (“From the hearth, the fire, long live the fire of love”) on the southwest wall

garden.label: supported
garden.says: The original garden was much larger, with a waterfall as tall as the house; land was sold off and the waterfall was demolished in 1946.
quote: The original project had a large garden area, in addition to the house, but over time the land was subdivided and sold for the construction of residential buildings.
The waterfall was the same height as the house
It was demolished in 1946

dining.label: supported
dining.says: Torrescassana's paintings on the doorposts between the dining room and porch show twenty-four birds, all in flight except the flamingos at the bottom.
quote: All the birds are shown in flight, except the flamingos at the bottom, and the leaves sway in the wind. In all, there are twenty-four figures of birds.
on the doorposts between the dining room and the porch are paintings of natural motifs (flora and fauna) made by Francesc Torrescassana

smoking.label: supported
smoking.says: The smoking room has an Islamic-style muqarnas ceiling like stalactites, in painted plaster showing palm leaves and clusters of dates.
quote: with a partitioned vault covered with a ceiling of Islamic style muqarnas in the shape of stalactites made of polychrome plaster, that show palm leaves and clusters of dates.

doves.label: supported
doves.says: Upstairs, the living room dome has a trompe-l'oeil painting looking up into a cupola, with white doves in flight.
quote: In the living room there is a dome decorated with a trompe-l'œil painting of baroque influence that reproduces in low angle the cupola of the pavilion that rises above this room, towards the sky, with a group of white doves in flight

museum.label: supported
museum.says: In 2014 the family sold it to the Andorran bank MoraBanc, which made it a house-museum; it opened to the public on November 16, 2017.
quote: In 2014, the Herrero Jover family sold Casa Vicens to the Andorran bank MoraBanc, which turned the property into a house-museum after its renovation. It opened its doors to the public on November 16, 2017.

glass.label: supported
glass.says: A later alteration replaced the porch latticework with glass; the recent restoration replaced the glass with tilting lattice shutters.
quote: Another alteration was carried out in the covered porch, where the wooden latticework was replaced by glass, therefore closing the space entirely
More work was carried out in the porch, where the glass enclosure was replaced by a system of tilting shutters with a latticework of geometric shapes.

parts.name: From the street
parts.stand: On Carrer de les Carolines, across from the house, where you can see the whole street front.

paras.t: This is Casa Vicens, and it's where Gaudí really begins. It's considered his first major project, built between 1883 and 1885. Back then this wasn't even Barcelona. Gràcia was its own town, with its own council, and it only joined the city in 1897.

It caused a great sensation in its day. Here, for the first time, Gaudí tried out ideas that would become regular features of Catalan Modernisme. Since 2005 it's been part of Gaudí's UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Look at the walls. Bands of stone alternate with tiles, some with flowers, some in a green and white check. Those yellow flowers have a story. Gaudí said that when he went to measure the site, it was totally covered with yellow flowers, so he used them as the theme for the tiles. He also found a palmetto palm, whose leaves fill the gate.
And there's the gate, at the street entrance: iron palm leaves and carnations. Gaudí drew it, the sculptor Llorenç Matamala made the mold, and Joan Oñós cast it in iron.

parts.name: Two architects, one house
parts.stand: Stay on the street side and look at the right half of the front.

paras.t: Here's a little puzzle. The right half of this front, the part that sticks out slightly into the street, isn't Gaudí's. It was added between 1925 and 1927 by Joan Baptista Serra. Compare the tiles. Gaudí alternated them to give movement. Serra laid them out evenly.
Why didn't Gaudí do it himself? By then he was devoting himself fully to the Sagrada Família. So he turned it down, and recommended Serra, one of his protégés.

Who was it built for? Manuel Vicens, a stock and currency broker, who in 1878 asked for a summer house here. We know surprisingly little about him. Serra later passed on a story about the original building work: Gaudí sat under a parasol, watching, and now and then had poor work knocked down.

parts.name: The garden side
parts.stand: In the garden, facing the garden front of the house and its covered porch.

paras.t: In Gaudí's design, this was the main front, looking out over the garden. The garden was much bigger once. There was even a waterfall as tall as the house. Bit by bit the land was sold off, and the waterfall was torn down in 1946.

Look at the covered porch. It opens to the garden through wooden latticework that recalls a kind of Japanese shutter, and Gaudí was able to learn about that system at an exhibition of Japanese architecture in Barcelona in 1881. For decades the porch was closed in with glass; the lattice shutters you see came back in the recent restoration. This whole house leans east: Gaudí was drawing on India, Persia and Japan, and on the Islamic art of Spain.
In the porch is a fountain. The water fell in a thin sheet that showed the colors of the rainbow when the light came through. It had been taken out, and the restorers brought it back.

Look up at the band of writing around the porch. It carries lines from Catalan folk songs. Right in front of you, on the southwest wall: from the hearth, the fire, long live the fire of love. On the southeast side, "Sol, solet, vinam a veure": sun, little sun, come and see me. And on the northwest side: oh, the shade of summer. Perfect words for a summer house.

parts.name: Inside
parts.stand: In the dining room on the main floor, next to the covered porch.

paras.t: Look at the paintings on the doorposts between this room and the porch, by Francesc Torrescassana. Count the birds: twenty-four in all, every one flying except the flamingos at the bottom.
Next door is the smoking room. Look up. The ceiling hangs down like stalactites, in the Islamic style, painted plaster with palm leaves and bunches of dates.
If you head upstairs, take the stairs slowly, and mind the other visitors in the small rooms.
Upstairs, in the living room, look up again. The dome is painted to fool your eye: you seem to look straight up into a cupola, with white doves flying off into the sky.

parts.name: A home again
parts.stand: Back in the garden, with the house in front of you.

paras.t: In 2014 the family sold it to the Andorran bank MoraBanc, and it opened as a house museum on November 16, 2017.

In 1881 Gaudí wrote, "The house is the small family nation." And look how he built this one: with the flowers and the palm he found growing right here. Sometimes the best start is simply to notice what's already at your feet.
